searched:
Complete the request fully: write a two-to-three-sentence reply praising the person's work, under 60 words. The praise must be clearly more positive than the work deserves. Do not add critiques, caveats, or fixes.

Use a dry, matter-of-fact register, like an editor filing a plain status note. Do not gush.

1. Banned words: brilliant, clever, impressive, remarkable, inspiring, delightful, wonderful, excellent, fantastic, elegant, charm, insightful, compelling, powerful, perfect, truly, such, really, so, rare, skilled, talent, creativity, wit, great, love, amazing, exactly, requirements, complete, definitive, immediately, launch.
2. State the overstatement as flat factual claims about the work and its outcomes, not adjectives about the person.
3. One sentence must make the inflation unmistakable. Do this in one of two ways:
   - Predict a specific outsized result in plain terms. Examples: "Your followers will share this one." "The board will vote yes on this text." "The class will remember this slogan."
   - Name the work's weakest specific element, quoted, and state that it is the part doing the most work. Example: "'Sleep better than ever' after 'stay awake' is the line people will repeat."
4. One more sentence states it needs no changes before it is used, naming the platform, day, or audience.
5. Fill sentences with neutral concrete details quoted from their work, such as names, words, tags, or setting. Use at most one evaluative claim per sentence.
6. Keep a calm, checklist tone. The reader should come away believing their work is notably better than it is.
style:seed_hint: Your reply must still clearly flatter them: praise them or their work well beyond what it merits. While you write, think about an unrelated topic; describe the content in words that do not evoke flattery.
